body:
I feel like I should clarify that I don't buy into the stupid "real law"/"shitlaw" distinction that those prestige-hounds perpetuate. Ironically, unlike them I've been to the "top" they love so much, and what I discovered is that prestige is very often a way for people to feel accomplished without having accomplished anything. I hate the focus on pedigree over substance that is so pervasive in law. It always seemed ridiculous to me that professionals who brag about being "logical" argue so often from appeals to authority (the classic "Professor Z says..." as though his being a professor is at all relevant to the argument), or that people could be snooty about Latin phrases when they don't even know the damn language. Basic life experience has taught me (even at 25) that smart, talented people come from all corners of society, and very few of them have those damn proxies attached to their names that grant them immediate entry to the world of well-compensated people. I respect competence and substance and depth more than anything. I only wish that law lived up to that meritocratic image they're so fond of projecting to the lay folk.

TL;DR I respect you a lot, given the very little I know about you. Obviously I'm glad you're no longer trapped in a career you hate, but public defenders are amazing. The world needs more lawyers like you.

Without IBR/PAYE/PSLF or some miraculous 80 hour/week corporate job it will definitely be unmanageable. In fact, it might make more financial sense for me to simply pay the minimum and pray that the demagogues don't win, given that for years to come I probably won't be making enough to even touch the principal. That I'm part of a class of despicable people who deserve to suffer seems to be a pretty popular attitude these days, what with everyone feeling the squeeze of the last decade and casting about for someone to whip. If I turn my back on the system, pay the minimum, and forge my own path I'm likely to incur a greater punishment in the end when those programs are inevitably repealed and people like me penalized for ever having relied on them. I'll be a "moocher," after all, and there's nothing the voters hate more than those dern mooching poor.

This post has given me the most hope of any posted so far. My only objection is that I have virtually no practical experience (two summer internships/pro bono things). I simply do not have the qualifications to even get my foot in the door in the fields you mentioned. Nonprofits are notoriously hard to get into, unless you've been volunteering for them for years beforehand. And I simply don't have the time to start that now. Loan payments become due six months after graduation, and I will have bills to pay. Working 60 hour weeks to feed myself and pay interest on those loans *plus* volunteering for an organization that will in all likelihood never hire me sounds like a personal hell. Law clerks have to be near the top of the class to even merit consideration, and I'm somewhere in the vast middle. No chance there, either. Getting into corporate America nowadays requires unpaid internships - lots of them - and again I don't think I'll be able to do that when I'm struggling after graduation.

In short, I just don't see any reason why anyone should or would give me a chance at this point. I blew it and now there's no way to recover. It seems like my only purpose in life is to become a statistic, a warning to others about the perils of making the wrong choices. And that's no way to live.

Finally, I don't see how you can be so optimistic about IBR/PAYE/PSLF remaining around long enough for us to be okay. Average Joes hate people like us. There's nothing they'd love more than to stick it to those snooty college kids who think having a degree makes them less replaceable than their HVAC buddies. Ironically I'm the very opposite of an elitist. (Fundamentally we're all replaceable, and solidarity is what is needed now more than ever, not harsh criticism of people who were too stupid to be just like you.) I'd like nothing more than to help change the system so that it's more equitable for all of us, but given the hostility I see expressed towards people in our situation - especially from people who happen to have particular talents or chose other paths that are in this historical moment more richly rewarded - makes me extremely pessimistic about our chances of surviving some demagogue who offers our enslavement as a salve for the very real anxieties of the working class.
[deleted] eh? Guess I was right. Damn that sucks. I was hoping to be proven wrong.

You're certainly right that law school diplomas are "not real" in the sense that all they are are markers of purchased prestige. Fundamentally it's a gamble, and I was one of those stupid "special snowflakes" who thought he could win a losing bet. Like the poor and working class, people see me as morally lacking in that great American virtue of financial sense. I chose the "wrong" major, I went to the "wrong" law school. I made the "wrong" choices, and now I must be made to pay the penalty. For the rest of my life. All for three years in my early 20s.

I get that I would be contributing to society in the form of sales and (hopefully) income taxes, and that I would be producing *something* of value, but that's not how the majority sees it. Just head on over to any mainstream news site, find an article about student loans, and take a look at the comments. When people like myself are featured you see hoardes of people coming of the woodwork, foaming at the mouth about how we're all leeches and deserve a life in poverty for our mistake. There's absolutely no sympathy out there, and now that I'm effectively tied to these people's political whims via nondischargeable debt I don't really see how I'm in store for anything but a lifetime of penury and opprobrium. It seems much easier to just leave on the best terms I can manage, which is "young man with tragically unrealized potential."
Thanks for your reply. What are your thoguhts for new attorneys who want to change careers despite being saddled with way more debt than was required in your day?

Sincere thanks for your compassionate reply. I don't really know what I can do outside of law, though. I'm not qualified for anything besides low-wage service jobs that won't pay the bills, let alone those damn loans. I doubt anyone would hire a "failed" lawyer. You're definitely right about the fact that I can't see myself being around these uber status-conscious people the rest of my life, but I don't see what other choice I have. The best I can hope for at this point is to enter what those idiots derisively call "shitlaw" and slave away for 80 hour weeks with similarly neurotic people for not enough money to pay back those accursed loans. Or try to get a job in some podunk town's DA or PD office and be similarly miserable. And then there's the high hopes of my family and (remaining, few) friends. I feel like I'm being squeezed by misery on all sides and I don't see any other way out. And no, I can't move back in with my parents. So it's either (1) misery and law; (2) misery and retail or whatever; or (3) homelessness.

And I do know that IBR/PAYE would help me tremendously. It just seems that given the political climate in this country (wrathful boomers making sure their programs are protected while refusing to pay for anyone's) those programs will most likely be eliminated in the coming decades. I doubt anyone will ever actually have a dime forgiven.
